sentences.text: Labocania was a medium-sized carnivorous dinosaur.
Its skull bones were extremely sturdy, featuring frontal bones that were significantly thickened.
The upper jaw teeth curved backward gradually and had a flat shape, while the front teeth did not have a D-shaped cross-section.
Gregory S. Paul estimated the type species L. anomala to be 7 meters long and weigh 1.5 tonnes in 2010.
Molina-Pérez and Larramendi estimated L. anomala to be 8.2 meters long and weigh 2.6 tonnes in 2016.
The fossils were found broken apart, worn down by the elements, and spread across an area of about two square meters.

A joint expedition by the National Geographic Society and the Los Angeles County Museum of Natural History led by William J. Morris discovered Labocania fossils in Baja California, Mexico, in the summer of 1970.
A volunteer named Harley J. Garbani discovered a fragmentary theropod skeleton north of Punta Baja near Cerro Rayado.
Ralph Molnar described the type species Labocania anomala in 1974 based on these remains.
The species name means "anomalous" in Latin, referring to its distinctive morphology.
Rivera-Sylva and Longrich described the second species Labocania aguillonae in 2024 from the Cerro del Pueblo Formation in Coahuila, Mexico.
The specific name aguillonae honors Martha C. Aguillon, the discoverer of the L. aguillonae specimen.
Rivera-Sylva and Longrich described a second species, Labocania aguillonae, in 2024 based on fragmentary remains from the Cerro del Pueblo Formation in Coahuila, Mexico.
The specific name honors the specimen's discoverer, paleontologist Martha C. Aguillon.
The elements were found disarticulated and heavily weathered, scattered over an area of about two square meters.
The remains were mixed with the ribs of a hadrosauroid.
Labocania was initially considered an indeterminate theropod, with later studies suggesting possible affinities to tyrannosaurids, abelisaurids, or carcharodontosaurids.
Molnar (1974) noted similarities between Labocania and tyrannosaurids but did not assign it to a family, classifying it as Theropoda incertae sedis.
Andrea Cau (2024) recovered L. anomala as a carcharodontosaurid in a clade with Shaochilong.
Some classifications place Labocania within the family Tyrannosauridae.
Some classifications place Labocania within the tribe Teratophoneini.
Molnar noted similarities between Labocania and tyrannosaurids in the ischium but placed it as Theropoda incertae sedis in 1974.
In 2004, Thomas R. Holtz Jr. considered Labocania a possible tyrannosaurid but noted shared similarities with Coelurosauria and abelisaurid traits like thick frontals and a reclined quadrate.
The parent group for the genus is Teratophoneini.
Labocania lived during the Late Cretaceous period in Mexico.
The age of the L. anomala fossils is debated, with estimates ranging from about 73 million years old to as old as 93.6 million years old, though vertebrate remains suggest a younger date.
Labocania lived in North America during the Campanian stage of the Late Cretaceous, between 76 and 72 million years ago.
The holotype specimen was originally dated to the late Campanian, approximately 73 million years ago.
Recent research has provided contradictory dates, possibly as old as 93.6 million years, though vertebrate remains suggest a younger age.
In the description of the second species, L. anomala is dated to 75.8 million years ago and L. aguillonae to between 72.5 and 73 million years ago.
The genus lived from the Santonian to the Campanian stages, between 85.7 and 72.2 million years ago.
The affinities of Labocania remain uncertain due to the fragmentary nature of the fossil material.
Due to its fragmentary basis, the affinities of Labocania are uncertain.
Andrea Cau's 2024 classification of the taxon as a carcarodontosaurid was quickly set aside due to new data.
